title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open research intelligence for academic research organizations Every contribution, connected. Tessera builds your organization's research footprint from public data: people, publications, grants, and clinical studies, linked with the evidence behind every connection. Curators confirm links in seconds, and everyone can find who works on what, and who should meet. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub Starts from public data PubMed, NIH RePORTER, ClinicalTrials.gov, iCite, and ORCID. No HR feeds or integrations to begin. Evidence on every link Each connection records its source, the evidence for and against it, and who decided. Humans decide Automation suggests and curators confirm; decisi

title: Overview
heading: See why, every time
text: Every suggested link between a person and a paper comes with its evidence, weighed in plain language: the ORCID iD on the paper, the organization in the affiliation, a grant it acknowledges, shared coauthors, a different first name. Weights can be learned from your own decisions, and auto-accept switches on only where the measured precision allows. How suggestions are scored → Fast curation

title: Overview
heading: Curate in minutes, not months
text: The review queue puts strong matches first, grouped by person, with the matched author and their affiliation highlighted. Accept, reject, or defer from the keyboard; accept all of a person's strong matches in one step, and undo anything. The review queue → Expertise

title: Overview
heading: Who works on what
text: Ask in plain words, such as "memory T cells". Tessera reads the question through your organization's papers, shows the concepts it understood, and ranks people by what they actually publish, with the matching concepts on every result. Finding experts → Connections

title: Overview
heading: See the shape of your organization
text: Who works with whom, and how research areas connect. Groups are found from the network itself and named by what they work on; people who bridge groups are marked. Every graph has a list view with the same information. Connections → Opportunities

title: Overview
heading: Who should meet
text: Missed connections are people whose interests are alike but who have never worked together, with the topics they share and anyone who has worked with both. The unit matrix shows which units share interests but rarely collaborate. Missed connections →

title: Overview
heading: How it works
text: Connectors fetch public records into a Parquet lake. The evidence engine builds the directory and suggests links, each with its evidence; curators decide in the ledger; and the search index and discovery data feed a JSON API and a fast, accessible web app.

title: Overview
heading: Try it in a minute
text: Tessera needs uv , which provides Python 3.12 or newer. The demo builds an invented research institute, with about 100 people, their publications, grants, studies, and a curator's decisions: git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/tessera.git cd tessera uv sync uv run tessera demo uv run tessera --config demo/tessera.toml serve Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 . To set Tessera up for your own organization, start with Getting started .

title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from a fresh checkout to a running Tessera with your organization's public research footprint: people, publications, grants, and clinical studies, connected with evidence. It takes about 15 minutes of your time; the first sync then runs on its own for a few minutes to an hour, depending on the size of the organization.

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: A Mac, Linux, or Windows machine (a laptop is fine) with internet access to the public sources: NCBI (PubMed and iCite), NIH RePORTER, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ORCID. uv , which installs the right Python (3.12 or newer) and Tessera's dependencies for you. Disk space: about 100 MB for a mid-sized research institute (a few thousand papers over five years), and a few gigabytes for a large academic medical center. Everything lives in one folder, the data home . Tessera needs no institutional systems, accounts, or credentials. An NCBI API key is optional and makes PubMed requests faster (see Configuration ).

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/tessera.git cd tessera uv sync Then create a configuration file and a data home: uv run tessera init This writes tessera.toml in the current folder and creates ./var for data. Run uv run tessera doctor at any time to check the installation.

title: Getting started
heading: Try the demo first (optional)
text: To see Tessera working before you describe your own organization, build the demo, an invented research institute with about 100 people, their publications, grants, and studies, and a curator's decisions: uv run tessera demo # builds ./demo in a few seconds uv run tessera --config demo/tessera.toml serve Everyone and everything in it is invented. Delete the demo folder when you are done; it is separate from your own installation.

title: Getting started
heading: Describe your organization
text: Tessera finds your organization in public records by name, so the [organization] section of tessera.toml matters more than anything else. Open the file and fill in: name : the organization's full name, such as "Example University" . aliases : every way the name is written in publication affiliations and trial records. affiliation_patterns : wildcard patterns for affiliation text, such as "example univ*" . reporter_org_names : the organization's name exactly as NIH RePORTER writes it on grants, usually in capitals. ctgov_org_names : sponsor and site names as ClinicalTrials.gov writes them. email_domains : domains such as example.edu , which count as strong evidence when they appear in an auth

title: Getting started
heading: Run the first sync
text: uv run tessera sync sync does everything in the right order: Fetches the organization's grants from NIH RePORTER, its studies from ClinicalTrials.gov, affiliated papers from PubMed, and papers linked to those grants. Builds the people directory: grant investigators, plus anyone on a roster you imported. Searches PubMed for each person by name, then fetches citation metrics from iCite and the public ORCID records of people whose ORCID iD it knows. Scores every candidate paper for every person and records suggestions with their evidence, along with links between papers, grants, and studies. Builds the search index the web app reads, and the concept profiles behind Find experts and similar peop

title: Getting started
heading: Open the web app
text: uv run tessera serve Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 . You will find: Home: counts, recent publications, publications by year, the largest active grants, and how fresh each source is. People, Publications, Grants, Studies: browse with search and filters. Every link between a person and a record carries a status mark ( Confirmed or Suggested , with how likely it is); select it to see the evidence. Find experts: who works on a topic, described in your own words, with the concepts behind every answer. See Finding experts . Connections: who works with whom, a person's topics and who shares them, how research areas connect, missed connections, and units compared. Review queue: suggested authorships in

title: Getting started
heading: Optional: import a roster
text: If you have a list of people (from a department page, a grant office, or a spreadsheet), import it to add people grant records would miss and to attach ORCID iDs, emails, and units: uv run tessera people import roster.csv The CSV needs a header row. Recognized columns are name (or family and given ), email , orcid , local_id , unit , unit_code , title , start , and end , with common spellings such as last_name , first_name , department , or start_date also understood; other columns are ignored. Dates may be a year ( 2015 ), a month ( 2015-07 ), or a day ( 2015-07-01 ). title: Describing your organization
heading: Describing your organization
text: Describing your organization Tessera has no HR feed. It recognizes your organization in public records by how the organization's name is written there: in author affiliations on papers, on NIH grants, and in clinical trial registrations. The [organization] section of tessera.toml is that description, and it decides what Tessera finds. A good profile finds nearly everything that belongs to you and very little that does not. This guide explains each setting, how to find the right values, and how to check the result.

title: Describing your organization
heading: The settings
text: [organization] name = "Example University" short_name = "EXU" aliases = [ "Example University", "Example Univ", "Example University School of Medicine", ] affiliation_patterns = ["example univ*", "exu medical center"] reporter_org_names = ["EXAMPLE UNIVERSITY"] ctgov_org_names = ["Example University", "Example University Medical Center"] email_domains = ["example.edu"] exclusions = ["Example University of Technology"] Setting Used for Notes name Display, and as an alias Required short_name Display in the sidebar Optional aliases Recognizing the organization in affiliations, sponsor and site names, and grant records; the PubMed affiliation sweep Whole words, case-, accent-, and punctuation-in

title: Describing your organization
heading: Finding the right names
text: Affiliations ( aliases , affiliation_patterns ). Search PubMed for your organization with the affiliation field, for example "Example University"[ad] , open a dozen recent papers, and note every form the name takes: abbreviations, former names, the medical school or hospital, and common misspellings. Include names of hospitals and institutes that belong to you, and leave out partners that do not. Grants ( reporter_org_names ). Search NIH RePORTER for a project you know is yours and copy the organization name exactly as it appears under Organization . Large organizations often have several (a university and its medical school, for instance); list each. Studies ( ctgov_org_names ). Search Clin

title: Describing your organization
heading: Checking the result
text: After uv run tessera sync : uv run tessera runs shows how many records each source returned. A RePORTER sweep that finds nothing usually means reporter_org_names does not match RePORTER's spelling. On the Sources page, the Found column shows the same counts, and the run notes say if PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov reported anything unusual. The Grants list should show your active NIH awards; spot-check a few you know. Discovered people lists affiliated authors who are not in the directory. If many of them clearly belong to another organization, an alias or pattern is too broad: tighten it or add an exclusion. On a paper's page, the Record card shows which source it came from. heading: How people are found
text: The directory starts from three sources: NIH grant investigators. Contact principal investigators on your organization's own awards join as active members. Other investigators (on multi-PI grants and subprojects, often from other organizations) start as discovered people and are promoted automatically once at least discover_min_papers of their papers carry your affiliation with their full name. A roster , if you import one ( uv run tessera people import roster.csv ). Roster people are members: active, or former once every membership the roster lists has ended. title: Curating
heading: Curating
text: Curating Tessera suggests; people decide. Every link between a person and a paper starts as a suggestion with a likelihood and the evidence behind it. Curators confirm or reject suggestions, and those decisions are permanent: later syncs add evidence but never change a decision. This guide covers the review queue, discovered people, and the tools around them.

title: Curating
heading: How suggestions are scored
text: For each person, Tessera looks at every paper with a compatible author name and adds up evidence for and against a match. Each item of evidence carries a weight and a plain-language explanation, for example: For: the author's ORCID iD matches the person's; the paper is listed on the person's public ORCID record; the same ORCID iD appears on the person's other papers; an email at your domain; your organization in the affiliation; the paper acknowledges the person's grant; coauthors who also appear on the person's other papers; the full first name matches; the paper's topics fit the person's work; a journal they publish in. Against: a different ORCID iD, or one you marked as not theirs; a diff

title: Curating
heading: The review queue
text: Open Review queue in the sidebar. Suggestions are listed on the left in priority order: strong matches first, grouped by person so they can be confirmed quickly, then possible matches with conflicting evidence, then ambiguous names. The panel on the right shows the selected suggestion: the paper, the author list with the matched position highlighted and its affiliation on that paper, the likelihood, each item of evidence with its weight, and the history of decisions. The review queue Key Action j or ↓ Next suggestion k or ↑ Previous suggestion a Accept: this person wrote this paper r Reject: someone else with a similar name d Defer: decide later (leaves the queue, kept on the person's profil

title: Curating
heading: Discovered people
text: Discovered people lists authors and investigators found in the data who are not in the directory: authors whose papers carry your affiliation but who match nobody you know, and co-investigators on your grants. For each, the evidence is shown: how many affiliated papers, over which years, recent titles, NIH grants, and the affiliation as printed. Promote someone who belongs to the organization. They join the directory, and their papers are suggested at the next tessera resolve or tessera sync . Dismiss someone who does not. They leave the list and are not proposed again by later syncs. Select several people to promote or dismiss them together. The Promoted and Dismissed views list past decisi

title: Curating
heading: On a person's profile
text: Review suggestions opens the queue for that person alone. Every paper, grant, and study carries a status mark; select it to open the evidence and accept, reject, defer, or undo. Add a publication attaches a paper the evidence engine missed, by its PubMed ID. Tessera fetches the paper from PubMed if needed and records it as confirmed, entered by you. The History tab lists every decision about the person's links. Identifiers lists the person's ORCID iDs and other identifiers, described in the section on ORCID iDs below. Memberships lists the person's units, with titles and dates, current ones first. Merge… folds another record of the same person into this one, or this one into it; see the next

title: Curating
heading: Possible duplicates
text: The same person sometimes has two records, typically one from a roster and one from grant records, when the roster row shares no identifier with the grant record. Possible duplicates lists pairs that look like one person, side by side, with the evidence: a shared identifier, the same author positions claimed on the same papers, agreeing names. A name alone never proposes a pair. Merge into… moves the left record's papers, grants, units, names, and identifiers to the record on the right, which is kept. Keep … instead merges the other way. Different people keeps the two apart; the pair is not proposed again. Later sets it aside. If both records had decided the same paper differently, the more

title: Curating
heading: ORCID iDs
text: An ORCID iD is the strongest evidence Tessera has: a researcher's own identifier, printed on many papers. When an iD appears at a person's author position on at least two of their likely papers, Tessera suggests it on their profile, under Identifiers , with how many of their papers carry it and, once it has been read, what the public ORCID record says. Tessera never confirms an iD on its own. Confirm makes the iD the person's. From the next sync, papers carrying it match decisively, papers listed on the person's ORCID record count as strong evidence (and are fetched from PubMed if Tessera lacks them), and papers carrying a different iD count against. Not theirs keeps the iD on record as some

title: Curating
heading: Learned weights and auto-accept
text: Admin → Evidence shows how suggestions are scored and how well, measured on your own decisions. Curators can look; admins can change it. Evaluate now fits learned weights to your accept and reject decisions and compares them with the hand-set ones on people left out of the fit. Once there are enough decisions (200, with 20 rejections, about 5 people) and the learned model predicts better, Release it makes it active from the next sync; Use hand-set weights goes back. Auto-accept can be switched on only at a score where the evaluation measured at least 99% precision over at least 50 decisions. Each sync then accepts open suggestions at or above it that have no conflicting evidence. They are ma

title: Curating
heading: The decision log
text: Decision log lists every decision across the organization, newest first: what was decided, about which person and record, by whom, when, and with what note. Link decisions open their evidence, where the latest decision can be undone. Decisions are never deleted. Undo is itself a recorded decision that restores the previous state, so the log always shows the full story.

title: Curating
heading: What survives a sync
text: A decision locks the link: later syncs and rescoring never change an accepted or rejected status. If a source stops reporting a link (a grant drops a paper, for instance), the link is marked as no longer reported rather than deleted. Dismissed people stay dismissed; promoted people stay members. Search and lists reflect decisions on the next request. Topic summaries on profiles refresh at the next sync.

title: Curating
heading: Who decides
text: With accounts on, every decision is recorded under the name of the person who signed in, and each person decides only what their role allows: curators for everyone or for one unit or person, researchers for the suggestions about themselves (their queue is My suggestions ). Without accounts (single-operator mode, on this machine only), every decision is recorded under the [server] operator name. See Accounts and sign-in .

title: Finding experts
heading: Finding experts
text: Finding experts Tessera describes each person's research with the MeSH headings that PubMed indexers attach to their papers. From those it answers "who works on this?", lists people with similar interests on every profile, draws who works with whom, and shows exactly what drives each person's topics. This guide explains what you see and how it is built.

title: Finding experts
heading: Who works on…?
text: Open Find experts in the sidebar (or press / and type "experts") and describe a topic in your own words: a disease, a method, a cell type, a question. Tessera reads your words through the papers they find. It searches the organization's papers, gathers the MeSH headings those papers share, and turns them into a small set of concepts. They are shown above the results as Understood as : Select × on a concept to drop it, if the search drifted somewhere you did not mean. Type in Add a concept to choose a heading by name, for example "Neoplasms", and add it. Select a concept on any result, or on a profile, to start a new search from that concept alone. People are ranked by how well their topics m

title: Finding experts
heading: Topics on a profile
text: Each profile's Topics card lists the person's most distinctive concepts. How this is built opens the full list, with, for each concept: its weight, relative to their strongest concept; how many of their papers carry it, and how many of those are confirmed; from keywords , when the concept comes only from authors' keywords on papers that have no MeSH headings yet. A concept counts for more when it is a major topic of the paper, when the person is first or last author, and when the paper is recent: weight halves every five years. Concepts that many people in the organization share count for less, so the list shows what sets this person apart rather than what everyone has in common. Headings th

title: Finding experts
heading: Similar people
text: The Similar people card on a profile lists the people whose topics overlap most, with the concepts they share. Pairs are worked out when profiles are built, not when you look, so the list is instant. Similarity reflects the topics of people's papers. It says nothing about the quality of anyone's work or whether they are available to collaborate.

title: Finding experts
heading: Connections
text: Connections , in the sidebar, draws three pictures of the organization and lists two kinds of opportunity. Each picture has a List view with the same people, topics, and relationships as sortable tables, for keyboard and screen-reader use, or for copying. View Shows Use it to see Collaboration People. A solid line means they share papers, grants, or studies; it is thicker the more they share and the fewer others share it. A dashed line means similar interests without any shared work Who works together, and who might Person focus One person, their top topics, and the people who share those topics, gathered around them Who shares someone's interests, and around what Concept landscape Topics, l

title: Finding experts
heading: Missed connections
text: Missed connections lists pairs of current members whose interests are alike but who have never published, held a grant, or run a study together, most alike first. Each pair shows the topics they share, and, when someone has worked with both, that person, who might introduce them. Limit the list to one unit, or to pairs in different units, and choose how alike they must be. Missed connections

title: Finding experts
heading: Units
text: Units compares every pair of units (the 30 largest with at least two members, by default). In each cell, the shade shows how alike the two units' members are, and the inner square how much they work together, both per possible pair of people, so large and small units compare fairly. A strong shade with a small square marks units that share interests but rarely work together. Select a cell, or move with the arrow keys and press Enter, to see the people behind it, with what they share and whether they have worked together. The List view has every pair of units as a sortable table. Units

title: Finding experts
heading: Keeping it current
text: tessera sync rebuilds profiles, similar people, and the graphs at the end of every run. To rebuild them alone, for example after many curation decisions or a change to [discovery] : tessera build discovery Until profiles have been built once, Find experts says so instead of showing results.

title: Configuration
heading: Configuration
text: Configuration Tessera reads one file, tessera.toml . uv run tessera init writes a commented starting point; the same file is in the repository as tessera.example.toml . Every setting has a sensible default except the organization profile. Tessera checks the whole file when it starts and reports every problem at once, with the setting's name, so a typo never fails silently. Unknown sections and settings are errors too.

title: Configuration
heading: Where the file is
text: Commands look for the configuration in this order: --config PATH (or -c PATH ) on the command line; the TESSERA_CONFIG environment variable; tessera.toml in the current folder. Relative paths inside the file (the data home, logo files) are relative to the file's own folder.

title: Configuration
heading: Environment variables
text: A simple setting can be overridden by an environment variable named TESSERA_<SECTION>_<SETTING> , which is handy for containers and services: TESSERA_SERVER_PORT=9000 uv run tessera serve TESSERA_DATA_HOME=/srv/tessera/data uv run tessera sync TESSERA_LEDGER_URL="postgresql+psycopg://tessera@db/tessera" uv run tessera serve Secrets never go in the file. The only secret Tessera uses, an optional NCBI API key, is read from the environment variable named by [sources.pubmed] api_key_env .

title: Configuration
heading: [organization]
text: How the organization appears in public records. See Describing your organization for how to choose values. Setting Type Default Meaning name text (required) Full name, shown in the app and used as an alias short_name text "" Short form for the sidebar aliases list [] Names as written in affiliations, sponsor and site names affiliation_patterns list [] Affiliation patterns; * matches any run of characters in a word reporter_org_names list [] Organization names exactly as NIH RePORTER writes them ctgov_org_names list [] Sponsor, collaborator, and site names in ClinicalTrials.gov (falls back to aliases ) email_domains list [] Domains whose addresses count as evidence of membership exclusions li

title: Configuration
heading: [branding]
text: Setting Type Default Meaning product_name text "Tessera" The product's name in the sidebar and page titles theme text "tessera" The default color palette: tessera , harbor , or cassette accent_color color (none) Replaces the palette's accent: a hex value, a color name, or rgb() , hsl() , or oklch() logo_light path (none) Your logo, shown in the sidebar in place of the Tessera mark and name (SVG, PNG, JPEG, or WebP) logo_dark path (none) The logo for dark mode; the light one is used if absent show_powered_by true/false true The small "Powered by Tessera" line in the sidebar Palettes. Each palette has a light and a dark version, and every viewer can switch palettes and modes for themselves und

title: Configuration
heading: [data]
text: Setting Type Default Meaning home path "var" The data home: raw downloads, the Parquet lake, the ledger (with SQLite), the search index, and logs. See Running Tessera

title: Configuration
heading: [server]
text: Setting Type Default Meaning host text "127.0.0.1" Address to listen on. Anything other than this machine needs accounts = true port number 8000 Port to listen on operator text "Operator" Without accounts, the name recorded on every curation decision accounts true/false false Require sign-in with local accounts and roles; see Accounts and sign-in session_idle_hours number 12 A session ends this long after it was last used (1 to 720) session_max_days number 7 A session never lasts longer than this from sign-in (1 to 90)

title: Configuration
heading: [ledger]
text: The ledger holds people, links, and decisions. Setting Type Default Meaning url text "" Empty means SQLite at <data home>/ledger.db . For PostgreSQL: postgresql+psycopg://user@host/dbname PostgreSQL support needs the postgres extra: uv sync --extra postgres . See Running Tessera .

title: Configuration
heading: [sources]
text: Setting Type Default Meaning contact_email text "" Sent with requests to the public APIs, as their usage policies ask. Set it to an address that can be reached Each source has its own table, [sources.pubmed] , [sources.icite] , [sources.reporter] , [sources.ctgov] , and [sources.orcid] : Setting Type Default Meaning enabled true/false true Whether sync and ingest all use the source api_key_env text "NCBI_API_KEY" for PubMed, else "" The environment variable holding an optional API key An NCBI API key (created under API Key Management in your NCBI account settings) raises PubMed's request limit from three to ten per second, which shortens the first sync of a large organization considerably.

title: Configuration
heading: [sync]
text: Setting Type Default Meaning window_years number 5 How many years of history the first sync collects. Later syncs fetch only what changed

title: Configuration
heading: [evidence]
text: Thresholds for authorship suggestions. See Curating . Setting Type Default Meaning strong_threshold 0 to 1 0.95 Suggestions at or above this likelihood are strong review_threshold 0 to 1 0.60 Suggestions below this are unlikely and hidden by default store_threshold 0 to 1 0.05 Candidates below this are not recorded at all discover_min_papers number 2 Affiliated papers needed before a person is proposed under Discovered people, or a grant co-investigator is promoted Changing a threshold takes effect at the next tessera resolve or sync ; decisions already made are not affected.

title: Configuration
heading: [discovery]
text: Concept profiles and similar people. See Finding experts . Setting Type Default Meaning half_life_years 0.5 to 50 5.0 A paper's weight in a profile halves every this many years likely_weight 0 to 1 0.5 How much a strong suggestion not yet confirmed counts, relative to a confirmed paper. 0 builds profiles from confirmed papers only similarity_floor 0 to below 1 0.10 Pairs of people less similar than this are not listed as similar similar_per_person 1 to 200 25 At most this many similar people are kept for each person Changes take effect at the next tessera sync or tessera build discovery .

title: Running Tessera
heading: Running Tessera
text: Running Tessera Tessera is one Python application and one folder of data. This guide covers what is in that folder, how to keep data fresh, backups, upgrades, PostgreSQL, and what to check when something goes wrong.

title: Running Tessera
heading: The data home
text: Everything Tessera stores lives in the data home ( [data] home , ./var by default): var/ raw/ the public sources' responses, exactly as received, one folder per run lake/ normalized records in Parquet files, one folder per table ledger.db people, links, decisions, and run history (SQLite; absent with PostgreSQL) derived/ the search index and concept profiles, rebuilt from the lake and ledger logs/ logs, one JSON object per line These parts are not equally precious: The ledger is the only part that holds human work : people, decisions, notes. Back it up. The lake and raw downloads come from public sources and can be fetched again. Keeping raw/ lets tessera replay rebuild the lake without the

title: Running Tessera
heading: Keeping data fresh
text: Run uv run tessera sync on a schedule. After the first sync it fetches only what changed, so a daily run usually takes a few minutes. Each source's expected freshness appears on the Sources page, which warns when a source is overdue or its last run failed. A daily cron entry (Linux or macOS): 30 2 * * * cd /srv/tessera && /usr/local/bin/uv run tessera --quiet sync A systemd timer works the same way: run uv run tessera --quiet sync from the folder that holds tessera.toml , as the user who owns the data home. uv run tessera runs lists recent runs with their status and counts. A run that ends partial fetched some but not all of its batches; the next sync retries from the last complete checkpoin

title: Running Tessera
heading: Serving the app
text: uv run tessera serve Tessera listens on 127.0.0.1:8000 by default ( [server] host and port ).

title: Running Tessera
heading: Accounts and sign-in
text: Out of the box Tessera runs in single-operator mode : no sign-in, answering only on this machine, with every decision recorded under [server] operator . That suits one curator on a laptop. For several people, or for a server others reach, turn on accounts: Create the first admin (you are asked for a password of at least 12 characters): `` bash uv run tessera users add ada --name "Ada Okafor" --role admin `` Set accounts = true under [server] , and host to the address to listen on (for example 0.0.0.0 ). Put Tessera behind HTTPS, typically a reverse proxy such as nginx or Caddy that forwards to it, so that passwords and session cookies travel encrypted. Have the proxy pass the original host (

title: Running Tessera
heading: Backups
text: With SQLite, back up ledger.db with SQLite's own backup command, which is safe while Tessera runs: sqlite3 var/ledger.db ".backup 'backups/ledger-$(date +%F).db'" Copying the whole data home while no job is running also works. With PostgreSQL, use pg_dump as for any database. To restore, stop Tessera, put the ledger back, and run uv run tessera build search and uv run tessera build discovery to rebuild the index and discovery data from it.

title: Running Tessera
heading: Upgrading
text: git pull uv sync uv run tessera db upgrade # apply ledger migrations, if any uv run tessera build search # rebuild the index with the new version uv run tessera build discovery # and concept profiles and the graph tessera doctor and the web app's health check ( /api/v1/health ) report a ledger that needs db upgrade . Migrations keep every row: they are tested on SQLite and PostgreSQL with a populated ledger, upgrading and downgrading. Back up the ledger before upgrading anyway. The changelog notes anything that needs more than these steps.

title: Running Tessera
heading: PostgreSQL
text: SQLite suits one organization on one machine well. To keep the ledger in PostgreSQL instead: uv sync --extra postgres Then set [ledger] url = "postgresql+psycopg://tessera@dbhost/tessera" (or TESSERA_LEDGER_URL ) and run uv run tessera db upgrade to create the schema. Put the password in the standard PGPASSWORD variable or a .pgpass file rather than in the URL. The lake and search index stay in the data home either way.

title: Running Tessera
heading: Lake maintenance
text: The lake keeps earlier versions of records when sources update them. Occasionally: uv run tessera lake status # files and rows per table uv run tessera lake compact # rewrite each table to current rows only uv run tessera lake gc # delete superseded files older than 7 days

title: Running Tessera
heading: When something goes wrong
text: tessera doctor checks the configuration, the data home, the ledger schema, and the database engines Tessera relies on (SQLite full-text search and DuckDB); tessera doctor --online also checks that each public source can be reached. tessera runs and the Sources page show failed or partial runs with the source's error. Logs are in <data home>/logs . Add -v to any command for more detail. A source changed or was down: run uv run tessera sync again; completed work is not repeated. Search looks out of date: uv run tessera build search rebuilds it from the lake and ledger in seconds.

title: The API
heading: Conventions
text: Envelopes. A successful response is {"data": …, "meta": {…}} . Lists put paging details and facet counts in meta . Paging. Lists take limit (up to 200) and either offset or the opaque cursor from the previous page's meta.next_cursor , which is null on the last page. Sparse fields. fields=id,name returns only those keys of each list item. Errors are RFC 9457 problem details ( application/problem+json ) with a title , a status , and a plain-language detail . Search highlights in highlights mark matches with the private-use characters U+E000 and U+E001, never HTML. Escape the text, then replace those characters with your own markup. Identifiers. title: Changelog
heading: Changelog
text: Changelog All notable changes to Tessera are recorded here. Versions follow semantic versioning ; each wave of work ships as a minor release (wave 1 → 0.1.0, wave 2 → 0.2.0).

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: tessera demo [PATH] builds a complete installation for an invented organization, the Corvane Institute for Biomedical Research: about 100 people in 22 labs, 700 publications, grants, clinical studies, ORCID records, and a curator's decisions, so every screen has something to show. Identifiers are chosen so they can never be mistaken for real ones. It is also what the documentation's screenshots are taken from. Screenshots for the documentation are taken from the real app, serving the demo organization, in light and dark ( node docs/capture/capture.mjs ), and the diagrams are drawn as SVG ( node docs/capture/diagrams.mjs ). A product home page for the documentation site, figures in the guides

title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: In the person focus view, the person in focus stays at the centre, and topics are drawn larger than the people around them, so people gather around the topics they share.

title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: With reduced motion turned on, the graphs drew every node and label in black: a tiny transition on every element made the colors read back wrong. Reduced motion now turns transitions off. The collaboration graph's legend lists former members only when the graph shows one.

title: Changelog
text: Connections. Tessera now helps people find who works on what and who should meet, with the reasons on screen, and lets several people curate with their own accounts and roles. ORCID strengthens the evidence, duplicate records merge reversibly, and the evidence model can learn from local decisions. Highlights: ORCID records and iDs as evidence; possible duplicates and reversible merges; dated unit memberships; local accounts with admin, curator (for everyone, a unit, or a person), researcher, and viewer roles; learned weights evaluated on held-out people, and auto-accept only where the measured precision is at least 99%; the expert finder; concept profiles that show what drives them; similar

title: Changelog
heading: Evaluation
text: Pilot check against people's own ORCID works lists: Tessera reads an ORCID record only once the iD is confirmed, and none was, so the records behind the 49 suggested iDs are independent of every score. Of 193 papers that 39 people list themselves (within the pilot's two-year window), 95.3% were found as candidates (target 95%); of those, 97.3% are in the strong band and all are at or above the review threshold. Works lists measure recall, not precision: people list only some of their papers. Details are in spec/evidence-engine.md . Learned weights and auto-accept need curator decisions, which the pilot does not have yet. On generated decisions, fitting recovers the weights that produced them

title: Changelog
heading: Dependencies and licenses
text: No dependency was added or changed: the runtime dependencies and their licenses are as in 0.1.0 (MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0, and PSF, with certifi under MPL-2.0 used unmodified, and the optional psycopg under LGPL-3.0, not bundled). The web app still ships no third-party code, fonts, or images. The force layout, community detection, and betweenness are original implementations of published methods.

title: Changelog
heading: Upgrading
text: Run uv run tessera db upgrade to apply ledger migrations 0003 to 0006, then uv run tessera sync (or tessera build search and tessera build discovery ) to build the new discovery data. Breaking: listening on any address other than this machine now requires server.accounts = true . See Accounts and sign-in .

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Missed connections (DIS-08): pairs of current members whose interests are alike but who have never published, held a grant, or run a study together, with the topics they share and anyone who has worked with both. Filters for unit, pairs across units, and how alike. Profiles' Similar people now say whether each pair has worked together. GET /api/v1/graph/missed . Groups and bridges: the collaboration network is divided into groups by modularity, each named by its members' most distinctive topics and given its own colour; people who connect groups are ringed and listed by name with the groups they work with. derived/person_group.parquet . The unit matrix (DIS-09): every pair of units compared

title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: authorship/v1.2 : a full-name match on a first name of at most two letters, which many people share, counts for less (the near misses of the v0.1.0 pilot check). Breaking: listening on any address other than this machine now requires server.accounts = true (it used to be a warning). Without accounts, Tessera also answers only to requests addressed to localhost or 127.0.0.1 , and in both modes refuses changes that a browser sends from another site. Cassette's stripe is now a thin sunset gradient in both modes, and the hero's diagonal bands are faint pinstripes in the same sunset colors. Record-type colors no longer resemble status colors: grants are gold, studies raspberry, and Cassette's pub

title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: On SQLite, a migration that failed part way could leave some of its schema changes behind, because Python's driver did not put them in the transaction. Schema changes are now transactional and roll back whole (a test checks it). A person listed on several roster rows without any identifier became several people; within one file, such rows with the same full name are now one person. Keyboard hints on buttons were faded below WCAG AA contrast; they are now full strength. Resolving again rewrote hundreds of unchanged suggestions because tied topics were listed in a random order in their explanations; ties are now broken by name, and a second resolve changes nothing.

title: Changelog
text: The first release. Tessera builds an organization's research graph from public data, with the evidence for every link, and gives curators fast tools to confirm it. It runs on a laptop or a single server. Highlights: connectors for PubMed, iCite, NIH RePORTER, and ClinicalTrials.gov; a people directory from grant investigators, an optional roster, and discovered authors; explainable authorship suggestions; links between papers, grants, and studies; a fast, accessible web app in three palettes with light and dark versions; a keyboard-driven review queue; a JSON API; and user guides.

title: Changelog
heading: Evaluation
text: Pilot check against ORCID iDs at a mid-sized research institute (70 directory members, about 2,400 publications over five years; 588 matched papers labeled by the ORCID iD printed on them): the strong band was 98.3% precise at 93.7% recall (target 99%), and suggestions above the review threshold were 97.9% precise at 95.8% recall (target 90%). Seven of the nine strong-band disagreements appear to be people with a second ORCID iD rather than wrong matches. Details are in spec/evidence-engine.md . Synthetic organization with known answers: the strong band is 100% precise with at least 99.8% recall, and candidate retrieval recall is 100%. Speed on the pilot: profile pages in 6 ms and search in

title: Changelog
heading: Dependencies and licenses
text: Runtime dependencies: Alembic, DuckDB, FastAPI (with Starlette and Pydantic), HTTPX, PyArrow, SQLAlchemy, and Uvicorn, plus psycopg for the optional postgres extra. All are permissively licensed (MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0, PSF), except certifi (MPL-2.0, used unmodified) and psycopg (LGPL-3.0, optional and not bundled), both compatible with distributing Tessera under Apache-2.0. The web app ships no third-party code, fonts, or images.

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Product specification in spec/ : vision, requirements, architecture, data model, data sources, evidence engine, discovery, UX, roadmap, process, glossary, and ADRs 0001–0008. Project skeleton: uv package, Apache 2.0 license, contributor guide. Configuration from tessera.toml with TESSERA_* environment overrides and validation that reports every problem at once. Data home layout ( raw/ , lake/ , ledger.db , derived/ , logs/ ). Ledger schema for people, names, identifiers, units, assertions, curation events, ingest runs, checkpoints, and settings, with an Alembic baseline migration tested on SQLite and PostgreSQL. Parquet lake with crash-safe writes, per-table manifests, current-version views

title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: Appearance has two choices under a new Appearance panel (and the command palette): light, dark, or system, and a color palette. Three palettes ship, each with day and night versions: Tessera (the default; its dark mode is now a neutral graphite instead of blue-navy), Harbor (deep navy, teal, bright blue, purple, and gold), and Cassette (label paper and rainbow stripes by day, black labels and a sunset at night). The organization sets the default with branding.theme ; each viewer can choose another. Every palette passes WCAG AA in both modes. branding.accent_color is now optional and, when set, replaces the palette's accent (lightened after dark, with text on it chosen for contrast). Decision
